# How to use this guide

Instrumental Methods of Analysis is a "draw and explain" subject. Almost every long answer asks for the **principle, instrumentation (with a block diagram) and applications** of one technique. Study one unit at a time: read the notes, draw each block diagram from memory until you can do it in two minutes, redo the worked calculations, then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short answer (5-mark) and long essay (10-mark) questions, rated by how often that kind of question appears in PCI-syllabus pharmacy papers.

The five units follow the five units of the PCI syllabus exactly. Unit 1 (UV-visible spectroscopy and fluorimetry) and Unit 2 (IR, flame photometry, AAS and nepheloturbidimetry) are long, so their notes are longer than the others.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with a block diagram and applications.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 UV-visible and fluorimetry | Electronic transitions, chromophores and auxochromes, spectral shifts, Beer–Lambert law with derivation and deviations, instrumentation (sources, monochromators, detectors such as PMT), multicomponent analysis, Jablonski diagram, factors affecting fluorescence, quenching |
| 2 IR and atomic methods | Modes of vibration, factors affecting frequency, sample handling, IR detectors (Golay cell, bolometer, thermocouple, pyroelectric), flame photometry and AAS principle, interferences and instrumentation, nephelometry vs turbidimetry |
| 3 Planar and column chromatography | TLC (methodology, Rf, detection), paper chromatography development techniques, column packing and elution, factors affecting electrophoretic mobility, gel and capillary electrophoresis |
| 4 GC and HPLC | GC instrumentation with detectors (FID, TCD, ECD), derivatization, temperature programming, HPLC instrumentation (pumps, injector, columns, detectors), N, HETP, Rs, van Deemter equation |
| 5 Special column methods | Ion exchange resins (classification, properties, mechanism, factors), gel chromatography theory and applications, affinity chromatography principle and steps |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Use one answer plan for every instrument question: **principle → block diagram → each component explained → advantages/limitations → applications**. Examiners give separate marks to the diagram.
2. Draw block diagrams as labelled boxes with arrows from source to readout. Put the detector at 90° for fluorimetry and nephelometry, and show the hollow cathode lamp and chopper in AAS.
3. Write the key equations with every symbol explained: A = εbc, A = 2 − log %T, ν̄ = (1/2πc)√(k/µ), Rf, N = 16(tR/W)², Rs, H = A + B/u + Cu, Ve = V0 + Kd·Vi, F0/F = 1 + Ksv[Q].
4. Comparisons are favourite short questions: flame photometry vs AAS, nephelometry vs turbidimetry, TLC vs paper chromatography, GC vs HPLC, fluorescence vs phosphorescence, normal vs reversed phase. Answer them as tables.
5. Learn the standard numbers: Na 589 nm, K 766 nm, D2 lamp for UV and tungsten for visible, quartz cells below 350 nm, paracetamol A(1%, 1 cm) 715 at 257 nm, quinine excitation about 350 nm and emission about 450 nm, Rs 1.5 for baseline separation, 3N − 6 and 3N − 5 vibrational modes.
6. Always end with 4–6 applications in drug analysis (assay, impurity, identification, bioanalysis); pharmacy examiners look for that link.
7. For practical-based questions, remember the reagent and wavelength of each BP705P experiment (see the practical guides).

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these with full block diagrams: **UV-visible spectrophotometer (with Beer–Lambert law and deviations)**, **fluorimetry (Jablonski diagram, factors, quenching)**, **IR (modes of vibration, sample handling, detectors)**, **AAS vs flame photometry**, **TLC**, **GC with detectors**, **HPLC instrumentation** and **ion exchange resins**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Equations to write without thinking**

| Equation | Use | Unit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E = hν = hc/λ; ν̄ = 1/λ | Energy of radiation | 1 |
| A = log(I0/I) = εbc; A = 2 − log %T | Beer–Lambert law | 1 |
| ε = A(1%, 1 cm) × M/10 | Converting absorptivities | 1 |
| Cx = (A2ay1 − A1ay2)/(ax2ay1 − ax1ay2) | Simultaneous equation | 1 |
| F = Kφ I0 εbc | Fluorescence vs concentration | 1 |
| F0/F = 1 + Ksv[Q] | Stern–Volmer quenching | 1 |
| ν̄ = (1/2πc)√(k/µ); µ = m1m2/(m1 + m2) | Hooke's law (IR) | 2 |
| 3N − 6 (non-linear), 3N − 5 (linear) | Vibrational modes | 2 |
| Rf = solute distance/solvent front distance | TLC, paper | 3 |
| µ = v/E = q/(6πηr) | Electrophoretic mobility | 3 |
| k = (tR − t0)/t0; α = k2/k1 | Retention, selectivity | 4 |
| N = 16(tR/W)² = 5.54(tR/W½)²; H = L/N | Efficiency | 4 |
| Rs = 2(tR2 − tR1)/(W1 + W2) | Resolution (1.5 = baseline) | 4 |
| H = A + B/u + Cu | van Deemter | 4 |
| Ve = V0 + Kd·Vi; Kav = (Ve − V0)/(Vt − V0) | Gel chromatography | 5 |

**Numbers and names worth memorising**

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| UV / visible range | 200–400 nm / 400–800 nm |
| Sources | Deuterium lamp (UV), tungsten-halogen (visible), xenon arc (fluorimeter) |
| Cells | Quartz for UV, glass for visible, 1 cm path |
| Best absorbance range | 0.2–0.8 |
| Transition order (energy) | σ → σ* > n → σ* > π → π* > n → π* |
| Polar solvent effect | π → π* red shift; n → π* blue shift |
| UV detectors | Photovoltaic cell, phototube, PMT, silicon photodiode |
| Fluorescence lifetime | About 10⁻⁹–10⁻⁶ s; phosphorescence slower |
| Quinine in 0.05 M H2SO4 | Excitation about 350 nm, emission about 450 nm; halides quench |
| IR mid region | 4000–400 cm⁻¹; fingerprint 1500–400 cm⁻¹ |
| IR sources | Nernst glower, globar (SiC), nichrome wire |
| IR detectors | Thermocouple, bolometer, thermistor, Golay cell, pyroelectric (TGS) |
| Na / K / Li / Ca emission | 589 / 766 / 671 / 622 nm |
| AAS source | Hollow cathode lamp of the same element; chopper |
| Releasing agent / ionisation suppressor | Lanthanum or strontium / caesium or potassium |
| Nephelometry vs turbidimetry | Scattered light at 90° vs transmitted light |
| TLC plate | Silica gel G (gypsum binder), activate 100–110 °C |
| Paper chromatography | Partition; Whatman No. 1; butanol : acetic acid : water |
| GC detectors | FID (organics), TCD (universal), ECD (halogens) |
| HPLC column | C18, 250 × 4.6 mm, 5 µm; Rheodyne 20 µl loop |
| Ion exchange resin | Styrene–DVB; capacity meq/g |
| Gel media | Sephadex (dextran), Bio-Gel P (polyacrylamide), Sepharose (agarose) |
| Affinity | Ligand + spacer arm on CNBr-activated agarose |

**Block diagrams in one line each**

- UV-vis: source → monochromator → sample cell → detector → readout.
- Fluorimeter: source → excitation filter → cell → (90°) emission filter → PMT.
- IR: source → sample/reference → chopper → monochromator → thermal detector.
- Flame photometer: nebuliser → burner/flame → filter → detector.
- AAS: hollow cathode lamp → chopper → flame or furnace → monochromator → PMT.
- GC: carrier gas → regulator → heated injector → column in oven → detector → data.
- HPLC: reservoir → degasser → pump → loop injector → guard + column → detector → data.

**Last-minute traps**

- Fluorescence is measured at 90°, absorption in line.
- Flame photometry measures emission; AAS measures absorption by ground-state atoms.
- In gel chromatography the **largest** molecules come out **first**.
- In reversed-phase HPLC the most **polar** compound elutes **first**.
- CO2 symmetric stretch is IR inactive.
- Paper chromatography is mainly partition; TLC on silica is mainly adsorption.

# Absorption maxima and effect of solvents on the absorption maxima of organic compounds

**Aim:** To record the UV absorption spectrum of an organic compound, find its absorption maximum (λmax), and study how the λmax changes in solvents of different polarity.

> Quantities and compounds are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves; keep organic solvents away from flames.

## Principle

When a molecule absorbs UV or visible light, electrons move from bonding or non-bonding orbitals to antibonding orbitals (π → π*, n → π*). The wavelength of greatest absorption is λmax. The solvent changes the energy gap:

- **π → π* bands** move to a **longer** wavelength (bathochromic shift) in more polar solvents, because the polar excited state is stabilised more than the ground state.
- **n → π* bands** move to a **shorter** wavelength (hypsochromic shift) in polar, hydrogen-bonding solvents, because the lone pair in the ground state is stabilised.
- Polar solvents also smooth out vibrational fine structure.

Each solvent must be transparent above its cut-off wavelength (water about 190 nm, methanol and ethanol about 205–210 nm, cyclohexane or hexane about 200–210 nm, chloroform about 245 nm).

## Requirements

Double-beam UV-visible spectrophotometer, matched 1 cm quartz cells, volumetric flasks (10, 100 ml), pipettes; test compound (for example p-nitroaniline, benzoic acid, acetone or a drug named by the teacher); spectroscopic-grade solvents: hexane or cyclohexane, chloroform, ethanol or methanol, water (and 0.1 M HCl and 0.1 M NaOH for ionisable compounds).

## Procedure

1. Switch on the spectrophotometer 15–30 minutes before use so the lamps stabilise.
2. Prepare a stock solution of the compound (for example 100 µg/ml) in each solvent.
3. Dilute each stock to give a working solution (for example 5–10 µg/ml) so that the peak absorbance lies between 0.3 and 0.8.
4. Fill both cells with the pure solvent and record a baseline (blank) over the scan range (for example 200–400 nm; start above the solvent cut-off).
5. Replace the solvent in the sample cell with the working solution and scan the spectrum.
6. Note the λmax and the absorbance at λmax.
7. Repeat steps 4–6 for each solvent, rinsing the cell with the next solution before filling.
8. For an ionisable compound, record spectra in 0.1 M HCl and 0.1 M NaOH as well.

## Observations and calculations

> Example readings, for practice only — record your own.

| Solvent | Polarity | λmax (nm) | Absorbance at λmax | Shift compared with hexane |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hexane | Non-polar | 320 | 0.52 | — |
| Chloroform | Moderate | 340 | 0.55 | +20 nm (bathochromic) |
| Ethanol | Polar, protic | 365 | 0.58 | +45 nm (bathochromic) |
| Water | Most polar | 380 | 0.60 | +60 nm (bathochromic) |

**Molar absorptivity at λmax:** ε = A/(b × c). For a 5 µg/ml solution of a compound of M = 138 (c = 5 × 10⁻³ g/L ÷ 138 = 3.62 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L) with A = 0.58, ε = 0.58/(1 × 3.62 × 10⁻⁵) ≈ 16,000 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹. A value above 10,000 points to a π → π* band.

**Interpretation:** a steady red shift with rising solvent polarity and a large ε indicate a π → π* transition. A weak band (ε below about 100) that moves to shorter wavelength in polar solvents is an n → π* transition.

## Result

1. λmax of the compound in each solvent is: ___.
2. The band shows a ___ (bathochromic/hypsochromic) shift with increasing solvent polarity, so it is a ___ transition.

## Precautions

1. Use spectroscopic-grade solvents and never scan below the solvent cut-off.
2. Hold cells by the frosted sides; clean the clear faces with lens tissue.
3. Rinse cells with the next solution before filling; remove air bubbles.
4. Keep absorbance within 0.2–0.8 by dilution.
5. Close volatile solvents quickly to avoid concentration changes.

## Viva questions

1. **What is λmax?** The wavelength at which the compound absorbs most strongly; assays are done there because the curve is flat and sensitivity is highest.
2. **Why does a π → π* band shift to longer wavelength in polar solvents?** The excited state is more polar and is stabilised more, so the energy gap falls.
3. **Why does an n → π* band show a blue shift in water?** Hydrogen bonding stabilises the lone pair in the ground state, raising the energy needed.
4. **What is a solvent cut-off?** The wavelength below which the solvent itself absorbs strongly.
5. **Why are quartz cells used?** Glass absorbs UV radiation below about 350 nm.
6. **Name the shifts.** Bathochromic (red), hypsochromic (blue), hyperchromic (more intense), hypochromic (less intense).

# Estimation of dextrose by colorimetry

**Aim:** To estimate the amount of dextrose (glucose) in a given sample (for example dextrose injection or oral powder) by colorimetry using the 3,5-dinitrosalicylic acid (DNS) method.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Some laboratories use the anthrone method instead (blue-green colour read near 620–630 nm); the calibration steps are the same. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles and gloves.

## Principle

Dextrose is a reducing sugar. On heating in alkaline solution, its free aldehyde group reduces yellow **3,5-dinitrosalicylic acid** to orange-red **3-amino-5-nitrosalicylic acid**. The intensity of the colour is proportional to the amount of reducing sugar and is measured at about **540 nm**. The concentration of the unknown is read from a calibration curve of standard dextrose solutions (Beer–Lambert law, A = εbc).

## Requirements

Colorimeter or spectrophotometer, glass cuvettes (1 cm), boiling water bath, test tubes, pipettes, volumetric flasks; anhydrous dextrose (standard), DNS reagent (DNS with sodium hydroxide and sodium potassium tartrate), distilled water, sample.

## Procedure

1. **Standard stock:** dissolve 100 mg dextrose in water and make up to 100 ml (1000 µg/ml).
2. **Working standards:** pipette 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 ml of stock into test tubes and make each to 10 ml with water (100–500 µg/ml). Prepare a blank with water.
3. **Sample:** dilute the sample with water so that its concentration falls in the standard range.
4. Pipette 1 ml of each standard, the sample and the blank into separate tubes.
5. Add 1 ml (or the volume in your manual) of DNS reagent to each tube and mix.
6. Heat all tubes together in a boiling water bath for 5–10 minutes.
7. Cool under running water; add a fixed volume of water (for example 8 ml) to each and mix.
8. Set the instrument to zero absorbance with the blank at 540 nm.
9. Read the absorbance of each standard and the sample.
10. Plot absorbance against concentration and read (or calculate) the sample concentration.

## Observations and calculations

> Example readings, for practice only — record your own.

| Tube | Dextrose (µg/ml) | Absorbance at 540 nm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blank | 0 | 0.000 |
| 1 | 100 | 0.112 |
| 2 | 200 | 0.221 |
| 3 | 300 | 0.335 |
| 4 | 400 | 0.442 |
| 5 | 500 | 0.556 |
| Sample (diluted) | ? | 0.276 |

**Least-squares line:** A = 0.001109 × C + 0.0005 (r = 0.99996).

**Sample:** C = (0.276 − 0.0005)/0.001109 = **248 µg/ml** in the diluted solution.

If 1 ml of a 5% w/v dextrose injection was diluted to 200 ml (dilution factor 200), the injection contains 248 × 200 = 49,700 µg/ml ≈ 49.7 mg/ml = **4.97% w/v**, that is 4.97/5 × 100 = **99.4%** of the label claim.

## Result

The given sample contains ___ µg/ml (___% w/v) of dextrose, which is ___% of the labelled amount.

## Precautions

1. Heat standards and samples together for exactly the same time.
2. Cool all tubes to room temperature before reading.
3. Use clean, dry glassware; traces of other reducing substances give high results.
4. Keep the sample within the linear range; dilute if its absorbance exceeds the top standard.
5. DNS reagent is irritant and alkaline; avoid skin contact.

## Viva questions

1. **Why does dextrose react with DNS?** It is a reducing sugar with a free aldehyde (hemiacetal) group.
2. **What colour is formed and where is it read?** Orange-red 3-amino-5-nitrosalicylic acid, read near 540 nm.
3. **Why use a calibration curve?** The reaction does not follow a fixed absorptivity value, so standards treated the same way are needed.
4. **Difference between colorimeter and spectrophotometer?** A colorimeter uses filters (wide band); a spectrophotometer uses a monochromator (narrow band).
5. **Name another colorimetric method for glucose.** Anthrone method or glucose oxidase–peroxidase method.
6. **Why is a blank used?** To cancel the colour of the reagent and the solvent.

# Estimation of sulfanilamide by colorimetry (Bratton–Marshall reaction)

**Aim:** To estimate sulfanilamide in a given sample by diazotisation and coupling with N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine (Bratton–Marshall reaction).

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles and gloves.

## Principle

Sulfanilamide has a free primary aromatic amino group. In acid solution it reacts with nitrous acid (from sodium nitrite and HCl) to form a **diazonium salt**. Excess nitrous acid is destroyed with **ammonium sulphamate**, because it would otherwise react with the coupling reagent. The diazonium salt is then coupled with **N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine dihydrochloride** to give a stable **magenta (purple-red) azo dye**, read at about **540–545 nm**. The absorbance follows Beer's law, and the concentration of the sample is read from a calibration curve.

```text
 Ar-NH2 + HNO2 + HCl  --(0-5 °C or room temp, acid)-->  Ar-N2+ Cl-  (diazonium salt)
 excess HNO2 + NH4SO3NH2  -->  N2 + H2SO4 + ...  (removed)
 Ar-N2+ + naphthylethylenediamine  -->  Ar-N=N-naphthyl (magenta azo dye, ~545 nm)
```

## Requirements

Colorimeter or spectrophotometer, cuvettes, volumetric flasks (100 ml, 25 ml), pipettes; sulfanilamide (standard), 1 M (or 4 M, as per manual) HCl, 0.1% w/v sodium nitrite (freshly made), 0.5% w/v ammonium sulphamate, 0.1% w/v N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine dihydrochloride, distilled water, sample.

## Procedure

1. **Stock:** dissolve 100 mg sulfanilamide in water (warm if needed, a little HCl helps) and make up to 100 ml (1000 µg/ml); dilute 1 ml to 100 ml to obtain 10 µg/ml working stock.
2. Pipette 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 ml of working stock into 25 ml (or 10 ml as per manual) volumetric flasks; this gives a series of standards. Prepare the sample in the same way so that its concentration lies inside the range. Prepare a reagent blank with water.
3. To each flask add 1 ml HCl and 1 ml sodium nitrite; mix and keep 3 minutes.
4. Add 1 ml ammonium sulphamate; mix and keep 2 minutes (effervescence of nitrogen).
5. Add 1 ml N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine solution; mix and allow 5–10 minutes for full colour.
6. Make up to volume with water.
7. Measure the absorbance at about 545 nm against the blank.
8. Plot the calibration curve and find the sample concentration.

## Observations and calculations

> Example readings, for practice only — record your own. Concentrations are the final concentrations in the measured solution.

| Solution | Sulfanilamide (µg/ml) | Absorbance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blank | 0 | 0.000 |
| S1 | 2 | 0.118 |
| S2 | 4 | 0.235 |
| S3 | 6 | 0.351 |
| S4 | 8 | 0.470 |
| S5 | 10 | 0.586 |
| Sample | ? | 0.402 |

**Least-squares line:** A = 0.05855 × C + 0.0007 (r = 0.99999).

**Sample:** C = (0.402 − 0.0007)/0.05855 = **6.85 µg/ml**.

Multiply by the dilution factor to get the amount in the original sample, then express as % of the stated amount.

## Result

The given sample contains ___ µg/ml (or ___ mg per tablet) of sulfanilamide.

## Precautions

1. Use freshly prepared sodium nitrite solution.
2. Keep the timing between additions the same for all flasks.
3. Make sure all excess nitrite is destroyed before adding the coupling reagent, otherwise the blank becomes coloured.
4. Read within the time the colour is stable (as per manual).
5. Avoid contamination with other aromatic amines.

## Viva questions

1. **Which group of sulfanilamide reacts?** The free primary aromatic amine (–NH2) group.
2. **Why is ammonium sulphamate added?** To destroy excess nitrous acid, which would react with the coupling agent.
3. **Name the coupling agent.** N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine dihydrochloride (Bratton–Marshall reagent).
4. **What other drugs can be estimated this way?** Other sulphonamides, procaine, benzocaine, dapsone (primary aromatic amines).
5. **Why measure at λmax?** Highest sensitivity and least error from small wavelength changes.
6. **Can acetylated sulphonamides be measured directly?** No; they must first be hydrolysed to free the amino group.
practicals.title: Estimation of sulfanilamide by colorimetry (Bratton–Marshall reaction)

# Simultaneous estimation of ibuprofen and paracetamol by UV spectroscopy

**Aim:** To estimate ibuprofen and paracetamol together in a combined tablet by the simultaneous equation (Vierordt's) method.

> Quantities and wavelengths are typical for a student batch. Determine the λmax values and absorptivities on your own instrument. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles and gloves; methanol is flammable and toxic.

## Principle

Both drugs absorb in the UV region and their spectra overlap, so one cannot be measured at a single wavelength without the other interfering. If the two do not interact, **absorbances are additive**. The mixture is measured at two wavelengths: λ1 = λmax of paracetamol (X) and λ2 = λmax of ibuprofen (Y). In methanol these lie at about 243–249 nm and about 221–222 nm respectively. With a 1 cm cell:

- A1 = ax1·Cx + ay1·Cy
- A2 = ax2·Cx + ay2·Cy

Solving the two equations:

**Cx = (A2·ay1 − A1·ay2) / (ax2·ay1 − ax1·ay2)**

**Cy = (A1·ax2 − A2·ax1) / (ax2·ay1 − ax1·ay2)**

where ax1, ax2 and ay1, ay2 are the absorptivities, A(1%, 1 cm), of pure paracetamol and pure ibuprofen at λ1 and λ2 (concentration then comes out in g/100 ml).

## Requirements

UV-visible spectrophotometer, matched quartz cells, volumetric flasks (100 ml, 10 ml), pipettes, Whatman filter paper; paracetamol and ibuprofen reference standards, methanol (AR or spectroscopic grade), tablets containing both drugs (for example ibuprofen 400 mg and paracetamol 325 mg).

## Procedure

1. **Standard stocks:** dissolve 10 mg of each drug separately in methanol and make up to 100 ml (100 µg/ml).
2. **λmax:** dilute each stock to about 10 µg/ml and scan from 200 to 400 nm against methanol; note λmax of each (λ1 for paracetamol, λ2 for ibuprofen).
3. **Absorptivities:** prepare 4–5 dilutions of each drug (for example 2–20 µg/ml); read each at both λ1 and λ2. Calculate A(1%, 1 cm) = A/c (c in g/100 ml) for each reading and take the mean (ax1, ax2, ay1, ay2). Check that each drug obeys Beer's law at both wavelengths.
4. **Sample:** weigh and powder 20 tablets; find the average weight. Weigh powder equal to one-tenth of the average tablet weight, shake with about 60 ml methanol for 15 minutes, make up to 100 ml, and filter (discard the first few ml).
5. Dilute 2.5 ml of the filtrate to 100 ml with methanol (dilution 2.5 → 100).
6. Read the absorbance of the diluted sample at λ1 and λ2 against methanol.
7. Calculate Cx and Cy with the equations and convert to mg per tablet.

## Observations and calculations

> Example readings and absorptivities, for practice only — record your own.

| Drug | A(1%, 1 cm) at λ1 (paracetamol λmax) | A(1%, 1 cm) at λ2 (ibuprofen λmax) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paracetamol (X) | ax1 = 650 | ax2 = 300 |
| Ibuprofen (Y) | ay1 = 30 | ay2 = 450 |

Sample absorbances: A1 = 0.553, A2 = 0.687.

Denominator: ax2·ay1 − ax1·ay2 = (300 × 30) − (650 × 450) = 9,000 − 292,500 = −283,500.

Cx = (0.687 × 30 − 0.553 × 450)/(−283,500) = (20.61 − 248.85)/(−283,500) = 8.051 × 10⁻⁴ g/100 ml = **8.05 µg/ml paracetamol**.

Cy = (0.553 × 300 − 0.687 × 650)/(−283,500) = (165.9 − 446.55)/(−283,500) = 9.899 × 10⁻⁴ g/100 ml = **9.90 µg/ml ibuprofen**.

**Back to the tablet:** dilution factor = 100/2.5 = 40, so the first 100 ml held 8.05 × 40 = 322 µg/ml paracetamol (32.2 mg) and 9.90 × 40 = 396 µg/ml ibuprofen (39.6 mg). The powder taken was one-tenth of a tablet, so per tablet: paracetamol **322 mg (99.1% of 325 mg)** and ibuprofen **396 mg (99.0% of 400 mg)**.

**Validity check:** (A2/A1)/(ax2/ax1) = 2.69 and (ay2/ay1)/(A2/A1) = 12.1; both lie outside 0.1–2.0, so the method gives reliable results.

## Result

Each tablet contains ___ mg of paracetamol (___% of label) and ___ mg of ibuprofen (___% of label).

## Precautions

1. Use the same matched cell for all readings, or check matching with solvent.
2. Measure absorptivities on the same instrument and same day as the sample.
3. Filter the sample solution; insoluble excipients scatter light.
4. Keep absorbances within 0.2–0.8.
5. Methanol is toxic and flammable; work in a ventilated area.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the basis of the simultaneous equation method?** Additivity of absorbance of non-interacting components (Beer's law).
2. **How are the two wavelengths chosen?** The λmax of each drug.
3. **What is an isosbestic point?** A wavelength where two species have equal absorptivity; used in the absorbance ratio (Q-value) method.
4. **Name other multicomponent methods.** Absorbance ratio, derivative spectroscopy, difference spectroscopy, HPLC.
5. **Why is methanol used?** Both drugs dissolve well and it is transparent above about 205 nm.
6. **When does the method fail?** When the spectra are almost identical, when the drugs interact, or when excipients absorb.
practicals.title: Simultaneous estimation of ibuprofen and paracetamol by UV spectroscopy

# Assay of paracetamol by UV spectrophotometry

**Aim:** To assay paracetamol tablets by UV spectrophotometry using its specific absorbance A(1%, 1 cm) at 257 nm.

> Quantities follow the usual pharmacopoeial method for paracetamol tablets. Use the current IP monograph and your lab manual where they differ. Wear goggles and gloves; NaOH is corrosive.

## Principle

In 0.1 M sodium hydroxide, paracetamol (as its phenolate) absorbs strongly at **257 nm**. The pharmacopoeial value of **A(1%, 1 cm) = 715** at this wavelength allows direct calculation of concentration without a standard curve:

**c (g/100 ml) = A / A(1%, 1 cm) = A / 715** (1 cm cell).

The concentration found is multiplied by the dilution factor to get the amount in the weighed powder and then per tablet.

## Requirements

UV spectrophotometer, matched quartz cells, analytical balance, mortar and pestle, volumetric flasks (200 ml, 100 ml), pipettes (10 ml), funnel and filter paper; 0.1 M sodium hydroxide, distilled water, paracetamol tablets (labelled 500 mg).

## Procedure

1. Weigh 20 tablets and find the average weight; powder them finely.
2. Weigh accurately powder equivalent to about **0.15 g** of paracetamol.
3. Transfer to a 200 ml volumetric flask; add 50 ml of 0.1 M NaOH, dilute with about 100 ml water and shake for 15 minutes.
4. Make up to 200 ml with water, mix and filter (discard the first 10–20 ml of filtrate).
5. Dilute 10 ml of the filtrate to 100 ml with water.
6. To 10 ml of this solution add 10 ml of 0.1 M NaOH and dilute to 100 ml with water.
7. Measure the absorbance at **257 nm** against a blank prepared in the same way without the sample (0.1 M NaOH diluted alike).
8. Calculate the content using A(1%, 1 cm) = 715.

## Observations and calculations

> Example readings, for practice only — record your own.

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Weight of 20 tablets | 13.000 g |
| Average weight per tablet | 0.6500 g |
| Weight of powder taken | 0.1950 g |
| Absorbance at 257 nm | 0.530 |

**Step 1, concentration in the final solution:** c = 0.530/715 = 0.000741 g/100 ml (7.41 µg/ml).

**Step 2, dilution factor:** two 10 → 100 ml dilutions, so 100. Concentration in the 200 ml flask = 0.000741 × 100 = 0.0741 g/100 ml.

**Step 3, amount in powder:** 0.0741 × 200/100 = **0.1483 g** paracetamol in 0.1950 g powder.

**Step 4, per tablet:** 0.1483 × 0.6500/0.1950 = **0.4942 g = 494.2 mg**.

**Step 5, % of label:** 494.2/500 × 100 = **98.8%**. (The usual IP limit for paracetamol tablets is 95.0–105.0% of the stated amount; confirm with the current monograph.)

Check: ε = 715 × 151.16/10 ≈ 10,800 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹.

## Result

Each tablet contains ___ mg of paracetamol, which is ___% of the labelled amount. The sample ___ (complies / does not comply) with the IP limits.

## Precautions

1. Weigh the powder accurately on an analytical balance.
2. Shake long enough to dissolve all paracetamol before making up to volume.
3. Discard the first portion of filtrate (adsorption on paper).
4. Use matched quartz cells and calibrate the wavelength scale.
5. Keep the final absorbance between 0.2 and 0.8.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is 0.1 M NaOH used?** It converts paracetamol to the phenolate, giving a stable, intense band at 257 nm and good solubility.
2. **What is A(1%, 1 cm)?** The absorbance of a 1% w/v solution in a 1 cm cell; for paracetamol at 257 nm it is 715.
3. **Why is no standard used?** The specific absorbance value is fixed in the pharmacopoeia; a reference standard can still be used to check the instrument.
4. **What is the relation between ε and A(1%, 1 cm)?** ε = A(1%, 1 cm) × M/10.
5. **What is a phenolate shift?** Bathochromic and hyperchromic shift seen when a phenol is ionised in alkali.
6. **Give the IP limit for paracetamol tablets.** Usually 95.0–105.0% of the stated amount.
practicals.title: Assay of paracetamol by UV spectrophotometry

# Estimation of quinine sulfate by fluorimetry

**Aim:** To estimate the concentration of quinine sulfate in a given sample by fluorimetry using a calibration curve.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles and gloves.

## Principle

Quinine is strongly fluorescent in dilute sulphuric acid. It absorbs UV light near **350 nm** (the 365 nm mercury line is often used in filter fluorimeters) and emits blue fluorescence near **450 nm**. For dilute solutions the fluorescence intensity is directly proportional to concentration:

**F = K φ I0 ε b c**

A calibration curve of fluorescence against concentration of standard solutions is used to find the unknown. Halide ions (chloride) quench quinine fluorescence, so HCl must not be used, and glassware must be free of chloride.

## Requirements

Fluorimeter or spectrofluorimeter, quartz (or glass for filter instruments) fluorescence cells polished on four sides, volumetric flasks (100 ml), pipettes; quinine sulfate, 0.05 M (0.1 N) sulphuric acid, distilled water, sample.

## Procedure

1. **Stock:** dissolve 10 mg quinine sulfate in 0.05 M H2SO4 and make up to 100 ml (100 µg/ml). Dilute 1 ml to 100 ml with 0.05 M H2SO4 (1 µg/ml).
2. **Standards:** dilute the 1 µg/ml solution with 0.05 M H2SO4 to give 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 µg/ml.
3. **Sample:** dilute with 0.05 M H2SO4 so that it falls in the standard range.
4. Set the excitation at about 350 nm (or select the primary filter) and emission at about 450 nm (secondary filter).
5. Set zero with 0.05 M H2SO4 (blank).
6. Set the reading of the highest standard to 100 (full scale) with the sensitivity control.
7. Read the fluorescence of each standard and the sample without changing settings.
8. Plot fluorescence against concentration and read the sample concentration.

## Observations and calculations

> Example readings, for practice only — record your own.

| Solution | Quinine sulfate (µg/ml) | Relative fluorescence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blank | 0 | 0.0 |
| S1 | 0.2 | 19.8 |
| S2 | 0.4 | 40.1 |
| S3 | 0.6 | 60.3 |
| S4 | 0.8 | 79.6 |
| S5 | 1.0 | 100.0 |
| Sample | ? | 54.0 |

**Least-squares line:** F = 99.95 × C − 0.01 (r = 0.99996).

**Sample:** C = (54.0 + 0.01)/99.95 = **0.540 µg/ml** in the measured solution. Multiply by the dilution factor to get the concentration in the original sample.

## Result

The given sample contains ___ µg/ml of quinine sulfate.

## Precautions

1. Use 0.05 M sulphuric acid, never HCl, and chloride-free glassware.
2. Keep all solutions at the same temperature; fluorescence falls as temperature rises.
3. Protect solutions from strong light; read promptly.
4. Do not touch the clear faces of the cell (all four sides are used).
5. Work at low concentrations; high concentrations give self-quenching and a curved plot.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is quinine measured in sulphuric acid?** Protonated quinine is strongly fluorescent; sulphate does not quench.
2. **Why is the detector at 90°?** To avoid transmitted excitation light reaching it.
3. **What are the excitation and emission wavelengths?** About 350 nm and 450 nm.
4. **Why is fluorimetry more sensitive than absorption spectroscopy?** Emitted light is measured against a dark background, not a small fall in a bright beam.
5. **What is Stokes shift?** Emission occurs at a longer wavelength than excitation because energy is lost by vibrational relaxation.
6. **What is a quencher? Example?** A substance that lowers fluorescence, such as chloride ions or dissolved oxygen.
practicals.title: Estimation of quinine sulfate by fluorimetry

# Study of quenching of fluorescence

**Aim:** To study the quenching of quinine sulfate fluorescence by chloride ions and to find the Stern–Volmer constant.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles and gloves.

## Principle

**Quenching** is any process that lowers fluorescence intensity. Halide ions quench quinine fluorescence mainly by **collision** with the excited molecule (dynamic quenching), taking away its energy before it can be emitted. For collisional quenching the **Stern–Volmer equation** applies:

**F0/F = 1 + Ksv [Q]**

where F0 is the fluorescence without quencher, F the fluorescence with quencher concentration [Q], and Ksv the Stern–Volmer quenching constant. A plot of F0/F against [Q] is a straight line with intercept 1 and slope Ksv. Bromide and iodide quench more strongly than chloride.

## Requirements

Fluorimeter, fluorescence cells, volumetric flasks (50 or 100 ml), pipettes; quinine sulfate solution (for example 1 µg/ml in 0.05 M H2SO4), sodium chloride solution (for example 1 M NaCl), 0.05 M sulphuric acid.

## Procedure

1. Prepare a series of flasks each containing the same volume of quinine solution (so that the final quinine concentration is the same, for example 0.5 µg/ml).
2. Add increasing volumes of NaCl solution so that the final chloride concentrations are 0, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03 and 0.04 M.
3. Make up each flask to volume with 0.05 M H2SO4 and mix.
4. Set the fluorimeter (excitation about 350 nm, emission about 450 nm); set zero with 0.05 M H2SO4 and 100 with the flask containing no chloride (F0).
5. Read the fluorescence (F) of each solution without changing the settings.
6. Calculate F0/F and plot it against chloride concentration.
7. Optionally repeat with KBr to compare quenching strength.

## Observations and calculations

> Example readings, for practice only — record your own.

| [Cl⁻] (M) | Fluorescence F | F0/F |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 100.0 | 1.000 |
| 0.005 | 88.9 | 1.125 |
| 0.010 | 80.0 | 1.250 |
| 0.020 | 66.7 | 1.499 |
| 0.030 | 57.1 | 1.751 |
| 0.040 | 50.0 | 2.000 |

**Stern–Volmer plot:** F0/F = 25.0 × [Cl⁻] + 1.00 (r = 1.000).

**Ksv = slope = 25 M⁻¹.** The chloride concentration that halves the fluorescence (F0/F = 2) is 1/Ksv = 0.04 M.

A linear plot is typical of a single (collisional) quenching mechanism; upward curvature suggests combined static and dynamic quenching.

## Result

1. Fluorescence of quinine decreases as chloride concentration increases.
2. The Stern–Volmer constant for quenching by chloride is ___ M⁻¹.

## Precautions

1. Keep the quinine concentration, temperature and acid strength the same in all flasks.
2. Use chloride-free water and glassware for the reference solution.
3. Read all solutions within a short time and at the same settings.
4. Rinse the cell with the next solution before filling.

## Viva questions

1. **Define quenching.** Any process that reduces the intensity of fluorescence.
2. **Types of quenching?** Collisional (dynamic), static (complex formation), concentration (self-quenching, inner filter), chemical, temperature.
3. **Write the Stern–Volmer equation.** F0/F = 1 + Ksv[Q].
4. **Why is HCl avoided in quinine assay?** Chloride quenches its fluorescence.
5. **How do temperature and viscosity affect collisional quenching?** Higher temperature and lower viscosity increase collisions and quenching.
6. **Practical use of quenching?** Estimation of halides, study of drug–protein binding.
practicals.title: Study of quenching of fluorescence

# Determination of sodium by flame photometry

**Aim:** To determine the sodium content of a given sample (for example a reconstituted oral rehydration salts solution or an intravenous fluid) by flame photometry.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual, the instrument instructions and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles; keep the flame area clear of solvents and paper.

## Principle

The sample solution is sprayed (nebulised) into a flame. The solvent evaporates, the salt vaporises and breaks into free sodium atoms, and some of these are excited by the heat of the flame. When they return to the ground state they emit yellow light at **589 nm**. A filter isolates this light, and a photodetector measures its intensity, which is proportional to the sodium concentration over a limited range. The unknown is read from a calibration curve of sodium standards.

```text
 [Sample] -> [Nebuliser] -> [Flame] -> [589 nm filter] -> [Photodetector] -> [Meter]
```

## Requirements

Flame photometer with sodium filter, fuel gas (LPG) and air compressor, volumetric flasks (100 ml, 1000 ml), pipettes, beakers; sodium chloride (dried at about 110 °C), deionised water (sodium-free), sample.

## Procedure

1. **Stock (1000 ppm Na):** dissolve 2.542 g dried NaCl in deionised water and make up to 1000 ml (2.542 g NaCl contains 1 g Na, from 58.44/22.99).
2. **Intermediate (100 ppm):** dilute 10 ml stock to 100 ml.
3. **Standards:** dilute the 100 ppm solution to give 10, 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 ppm Na.
4. **Sample:** dilute so that it falls within the range. For an ORS solution, dilute 2 ml to 100 ml (factor 50).
5. Light the flame as per instructions and let the instrument warm up; select the sodium filter.
6. Aspirate deionised water and set the reading to zero.
7. Aspirate the highest standard (100 ppm) and set the reading to 100 (or the maximum used).
8. Aspirate each standard and the sample in turn, aspirating water between solutions, and note the steady reading.
9. Recheck zero and the top standard at the end.
10. Plot reading against concentration and find the sample concentration.

## Observations and calculations

> Example readings, for practice only — record your own.

| Solution | Na (ppm) | Emission reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blank | 0 | 0 |
| S1 | 10 | 10 |
| S2 | 20 | 20 |
| S3 | 40 | 39 |
| S4 | 60 | 58 |
| S5 | 80 | 78 |
| S6 | 100 | 97 |
| Sample (diluted 1:50) | ? | 33.5 |

**Least-squares line:** reading = 0.966 × C + 0.42 (r = 0.99997).

**Diluted sample:** C = (33.5 − 0.42)/0.966 = **34.2 ppm Na**.

**Original sample:** 34.2 × 50 = **1712 mg/L Na**, that is 1712/22.99 = **74.5 mmol/L** sodium.

**As NaCl (if needed):** mg NaCl = mg Na × 2.542.

Note: the curve bends at high concentration (self-absorption, ionisation), so stay in the linear range.

## Result

The sample contains ___ ppm (___ mmol/L) of sodium.

## Precautions

1. Use sodium-free (deionised) water and clean plastic or well-rinsed glassware; sodium contamination from glass and fingers is common.
2. Let the flame stabilise and keep gas and air pressures constant.
3. Aspirate water between samples to clean the nebuliser.
4. Check zero and full-scale often; drift is common.
5. Matrix of standards and samples should be similar (viscosity, other salts).

## Viva questions

1. **At what wavelength is sodium measured?** 589 nm (yellow D line).
2. **What happens to the sample in the flame?** Desolvation, vaporisation, atomisation, excitation, emission.
3. **Name the interferences.** Spectral, ionisation, chemical, physical (matrix), self-absorption.
4. **Why use an internal standard such as lithium?** To correct for fluctuations in flame and aspiration rate.
5. **How does flame photometry differ from AAS?** It measures emission by excited atoms; AAS measures absorption by ground-state atoms.
6. **Give pharmaceutical uses.** Na in ORS, IV fluids, dialysis solutions; serum electrolytes.
practicals.title: Determination of sodium by flame photometry

# Determination of potassium by flame photometry

**Aim:** To determine the potassium content of a given sample (for example a reconstituted oral rehydration salts solution or potassium chloride preparation) by flame photometry.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual, the instrument instructions and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles; keep the flame area clear.

## Principle

Potassium atoms in the flame are thermally excited and emit radiation at about **766 nm** (the violet colour seen in the flame comes from weaker lines). A potassium filter (about 767–768 nm) isolates this emission and the detector measures its intensity, which is proportional to concentration over a working range. Potassium is easily ionised in hot flames, which lowers the emission; a low-temperature flame (LPG–air) is used, and an ionisation suppressor may be added. The sample concentration is found from a calibration curve.

## Requirements

Flame photometer with potassium filter, LPG and air supply, volumetric flasks (50, 100, 1000 ml), pipettes; potassium chloride (dried at about 110 °C), deionised water, sample.

## Procedure

1. **Stock (1000 ppm K):** dissolve 1.907 g dried KCl in deionised water and make up to 1000 ml (1.907 g KCl contains 1 g K, from 74.55/39.10).
2. **Intermediate (100 ppm):** dilute 10 ml stock to 100 ml.
3. **Standards:** prepare 5, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 ppm K.
4. **Sample:** dilute to fall within the range (for ORS, 2 ml to 50 ml, factor 25).
5. Light the flame, select the potassium filter and allow warm-up.
6. Set zero with deionised water and full scale (100) with the 50 ppm standard.
7. Read each standard and the sample, aspirating water in between.
8. Recheck zero and full scale; plot the curve and calculate.

## Observations and calculations

> Example readings, for practice only — record your own.

| Solution | K (ppm) | Emission reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blank | 0 | 0 |
| S1 | 5 | 11 |
| S2 | 10 | 21 |
| S3 | 20 | 41 |
| S4 | 30 | 61 |
| S5 | 40 | 80 |
| S6 | 50 | 100 |
| Sample (diluted 1:25) | ? | 62.5 |

**Least-squares line:** reading = 1.975 × C + 1.32 (r = 0.99997).

**Diluted sample:** C = (62.5 − 1.32)/1.975 = **31.0 ppm K**.

**Original sample:** 31.0 × 25 = **775 mg/L K**, that is 775/39.10 = **19.8 mmol/L** potassium.

**As KCl (if needed):** mg KCl = mg K × 1.907.

## Result

The sample contains ___ ppm (___ mmol/L) of potassium.

## Precautions

1. Use deionised water and rinsed plastic or glassware.
2. Keep gas and air pressures steady; let the flame stabilise.
3. Large amounts of sodium in the sample can raise potassium readings; match the standards with the sample matrix if needed.
4. Clean the nebuliser by aspirating water between solutions.
5. Work within the linear range.

## Viva questions

1. **What wavelength is used for potassium?** About 766 nm (filter 767–768 nm).
2. **Why does potassium show ionisation interference?** It has a low ionisation energy, so in hot flames some atoms become ions that do not emit the atomic line.
3. **How is ionisation interference reduced?** Cooler flame, or adding an ionisation suppressor such as caesium.
4. **Why do we use a calibration curve?** Emission is linear only over a limited range and depends on flame conditions.
5. **What detectors are used?** Photovoltaic cell, phototube or photomultiplier tube.
6. **Clinical relevance?** Serum potassium monitoring in kidney disease and diuretic therapy.
practicals.title: Determination of potassium by flame photometry

# Determination of chlorides and sulphates by nephelo-turbidimetry

**Aim:** To determine the concentration of chloride (as silver chloride) by nephelometry and of sulphate (as barium sulphate) by turbidimetry in a given sample.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles and gloves; silver nitrate stains skin.

## Principle

A fine, evenly dispersed precipitate scatters light (Tyndall effect).

- **Chloride** reacts with silver nitrate in nitric acid to give colloidal **AgCl**: Cl⁻ + Ag⁺ → AgCl. The intensity of light scattered at 90° (nephelometry) is proportional to concentration in dilute suspensions: Is = Ks × c.
- **Sulphate** reacts with barium chloride in acid medium to give **BaSO4**: SO4²⁻ + Ba²⁺ → BaSO4. The fall in transmitted light (turbidance) is measured in a turbidimeter or a colorimeter, often near 420 nm: S = log(I0/I) = kbc.

The particle size must be the same in standards and samples, so concentration of reagents, order of mixing, time, stirring and temperature are kept constant, and a **stabiliser** (glycerol–ethanol mixture, gelatin or gum) keeps the particles suspended.

## Requirements

Nephelometer (or fluorimeter used at 90°), turbidimeter or colorimeter, cells, volumetric flasks, pipettes, stopwatch; sodium chloride (dried), potassium sulphate or sodium sulphate (dried), dilute nitric acid, silver nitrate solution (about 0.1 M), barium chloride (crystals or solution), conditioning reagent (glycerol, ethanol, NaCl and HCl in water, or gelatin solution), distilled water, sample.

## Procedure

**A. Chloride (nephelometry)**

1. Prepare a stock of 100 ppm Cl⁻ (0.1648 g dried NaCl per litre) and standards of 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 ppm.
2. Into a series of 50 ml flasks put equal volumes of each standard and of the sample; add 1 ml dilute nitric acid to each.
3. Add 1 ml silver nitrate solution, make up to volume, mix the same way and keep in the dark for 5 minutes.
4. Set zero with a blank (water + reagents) and 100 with the highest standard.
5. Read the scattered light of standards and sample at 90°; plot reading against concentration.

**B. Sulphate (turbidimetry)**

1. Prepare a stock of 100 ppm SO4²⁻ (0.1814 g dried K2SO4 per litre) and standards of 10–50 ppm.
2. To equal volumes of each standard and sample add 5 ml conditioning reagent and mix.
3. Add a fixed amount of barium chloride (a measured spoonful of crystals or a fixed volume of solution) while stirring for exactly 1 minute.
4. Read the absorbance (turbidance) at about 420 nm against a blank after a fixed time (for example 4 minutes).
5. Plot absorbance against concentration.

## Observations and calculations

> Example readings, for practice only — record your own.

| Cl⁻ (ppm) | Nephelometer reading |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 |
| 5 | 12 |
| 10 | 24 |
| 15 | 37 |
| 20 | 49 |
| 25 | 61 |
| Sample | 30 |

Line: reading = 2.46 × C − 0.30 (r = 0.9999). Sample: C = (30 + 0.30)/2.46 = **12.3 ppm Cl⁻** (multiply by any dilution factor).

| SO4²⁻ (ppm) | Absorbance (turbidance) |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | 0.000 |
| 10 | 0.081 |
| 20 | 0.165 |
| 30 | 0.248 |
| 40 | 0.331 |
| 50 | 0.410 |
| Sample | 0.205 |

Line: A = 0.00824 × C − 0.0002 (r = 0.9999). Sample: C = (0.205 + 0.0002)/0.00824 = **24.9 ppm SO4²⁻**.

## Result

The sample contains ___ ppm chloride and ___ ppm sulphate.

## Precautions

1. Treat standards and samples in exactly the same way (volumes, order, stirring, time).
2. Read at a fixed time after precipitation; the suspension settles or grows with time.
3. Keep the AgCl suspension out of strong light (it darkens).
4. Use clean, scratch-free cells; dust and bubbles scatter light.
5. Use chloride- and sulphate-free water.

## Viva questions

1. **Difference between nephelometry and turbidimetry?** Nephelometry measures scattered light at 90° (dilute suspensions); turbidimetry measures transmitted light (denser suspensions).
2. **Why is a stabiliser added?** To keep particles small and uniform and prevent settling.
3. **Why is nitric acid added in the chloride test?** To prevent precipitation of other silver salts (carbonate, phosphate).
4. **What standard is used for water turbidity?** Formazin suspension; results in NTU.
5. **Which factors affect scattering?** Particle size, number, shape, wavelength and refractive index difference.
6. **Relation to IP limit tests?** The IP chloride and sulphate limit tests compare opalescence visually; this is the instrumental form.

# Separation of amino acids by paper chromatography

**Aim:** To separate and identify the amino acids in a given mixture by ascending paper chromatography and to calculate their Rf values.

> Quantities and solvent are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear gloves when handling the paper (fingerprints contain amino acids) and use ninhydrin spray in a fume hood.

## Principle

Paper chromatography is mainly **partition chromatography**. Water held by the cellulose fibres of the paper is the stationary phase; the moving organic solvent is the mobile phase. Amino acids distribute between the two according to their polarity: more polar amino acids stay longer in the water phase and move less, while less polar ones (with larger non-polar side chains such as leucine) move further. After development, the colourless amino acids are located by spraying with **ninhydrin**, which gives purple spots (Ruhemann's purple; proline gives yellow). Each spot is identified by its **Rf value** and by comparison with reference amino acids run on the same paper.

**Rf = distance travelled by the amino acid / distance travelled by the solvent front**

## Requirements

Whatman No. 1 chromatography paper, chromatography jar with lid, capillary tubes, pencil and ruler, hair dryer, oven (100–105 °C), sprayer; solvent: n-butanol : glacial acetic acid : water (4 : 1 : 5, upper layer after shaking and separating; or 4 : 1 : 1 as per manual); 0.2% ninhydrin in acetone or n-butanol; 1% solutions of standard amino acids (for example glycine, alanine, leucine), unknown mixture.

## Procedure

1. Prepare the solvent, place it in the jar to a depth of about 1 cm, close the lid and let the jar saturate for 30–60 minutes.
2. Cut the paper to size; draw a pencil base line about 2–3 cm from the bottom and mark points 2 cm apart.
3. Spot each standard and the mixture on separate points with a fine capillary; keep spots small (2–3 mm) and dry between applications.
4. Hang or stand the paper in the jar so that the base line is above the solvent level and the paper does not touch the walls; close the lid.
5. Develop until the solvent rises 12–15 cm (or near the top).
6. Remove the paper, mark the solvent front with pencil at once and dry it.
7. Spray evenly with ninhydrin reagent and heat at 100–105 °C for 3–5 minutes until purple spots appear.
8. Outline the spots, measure the distance from the base line to the centre of each spot and to the solvent front, and calculate Rf values.
9. Identify the components of the mixture by matching Rf values and colours with the standards.

## Observations and calculations

> Example readings, for practice only — record your own. Rf values change with paper, solvent, temperature and saturation, so always compare with standards on the same paper.

Solvent front distance = 15.0 cm.

| Spot | Distance moved (cm) | Rf | Colour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Glycine (standard) | 3.9 | 3.9/15.0 = 0.26 | Purple |
| Alanine (standard) | 5.7 | 5.7/15.0 = 0.38 | Purple |
| Leucine (standard) | 10.9 | 10.9/15.0 = 0.73 | Purple |
| Mixture spot 1 | 3.9 | 0.26 | Purple (glycine) |
| Mixture spot 2 | 10.8 | 0.72 | Purple (leucine) |

## Result

The given mixture contains ___ and ___ (Rf values ___ and ___).

## Precautions

1. Handle the paper only at the edges and wear gloves.
2. Draw lines with pencil, never ink (ink runs with the solvent).
3. Keep spots small and the base line above the solvent.
4. Saturate the jar and keep it closed during development.
5. Mark the solvent front immediately after taking out the paper.
6. Spray ninhydrin in a fume hood; avoid inhaling solvents.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the stationary phase in paper chromatography?** Water held by the cellulose fibres.
2. **Why is ninhydrin used?** It reacts with α-amino acids to give purple Ruhemann's purple; proline and hydroxyproline give yellow.
3. **Which amino acid moves furthest and why?** Those with larger non-polar side chains (leucine), since they are less polar.
4. **What is Rf? Can it exceed 1?** Ratio of solute to solvent-front distance; it is always below 1.
5. **What is two-dimensional chromatography?** Development in two solvents at right angles to separate complex mixtures.
6. **Why saturate the chamber?** To prevent evaporation from the paper and give reproducible Rf values.
practicals.title: Separation of amino acids by paper chromatography

# Separation of sugars by thin layer chromatography

**Aim:** To separate and identify sugars in a given mixture by thin layer chromatography (TLC) and to calculate their Rf values.

> Solvent and detecting reagent vary between laboratories (other common systems use ethyl acetate–isopropanol–water or chloroform–acetic acid–water). Follow your lab manual and your teacher. Wear goggles and gloves; spray and heat plates in a fume hood.

## Principle

Sugars are very polar and are held strongly on silica gel. On a thin layer of silica gel (sometimes impregnated with boric acid or sodium acetate to sharpen the spots), sugars separate by adsorption and partition with a polar mobile phase. Disaccharides (sucrose, lactose) are more polar and larger than monosaccharides (glucose, fructose), so they usually move less. Sugars are colourless and do not absorb at 254 nm, so they are made visible with a spray reagent and heating, for example **aniline–diphenylamine–phosphoric acid** reagent or **anisaldehyde–sulphuric acid**, which give coloured spots. Identification is by Rf and comparison with standards on the same plate.

## Requirements

Glass plates (20 × 20 or 20 × 5 cm) or pre-coated silica gel plates, TLC spreader, silica gel G, developing tank with lid, capillaries, oven (100–110 °C), sprayer, hot plate or oven for colour development; mobile phase, for example n-butanol : acetic acid : water (4 : 1 : 1 or as per manual); detecting reagent; 1% solutions of glucose, fructose, sucrose and lactose in water–ethanol, unknown mixture.

## Procedure

1. **Plate preparation:** make a slurry of silica gel G with water (about 1 : 2 w/v), spread a uniform 0.25 mm layer, air dry and activate at 100–110 °C for 30 minutes. (Pre-coated plates need only activation.)
2. Saturate the tank with mobile phase (filter paper lining) for 30 minutes.
3. Draw a light pencil line 1.5–2 cm from the bottom; spot standards and mixture 1.5 cm apart with fine capillaries; dry.
4. Place the plate in the tank (spots above the solvent), close and develop until the solvent is about 1 cm from the top (for long runs, develop twice after drying).
5. Remove the plate, mark the solvent front and dry in warm air.
6. Spray evenly with the detecting reagent and heat at about 105–120 °C for 5–10 minutes until spots appear.
7. Measure distances, calculate Rf values and identify the sugars in the mixture.

## Observations and calculations

> Example readings, for practice only — record your own; compare only with standards on the same plate.

Solvent front distance = 10.0 cm.

| Spot | Distance moved (cm) | Rf |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lactose (standard) | 2.1 | 0.21 |
| Sucrose (standard) | 3.0 | 0.30 |
| Glucose (standard) | 3.6 | 0.36 |
| Fructose (standard) | 4.1 | 0.41 |
| Mixture spot 1 | 3.0 | 0.30 (sucrose) |
| Mixture spot 2 | 3.6 | 0.36 (glucose) |

## Result

The given mixture contains ___ and ___ (Rf ___ and ___).

## Precautions

1. Spread an even layer and activate it; moist plates give poor separation.
2. Keep spots small; overloading causes streaking (sugars streak easily).
3. Saturate the tank and keep the lid closed.
4. Do not disturb the tank during development.
5. Handle acid spray reagents and hot plates with care, in a fume hood.

## Viva questions

1. **What does G in silica gel G mean?** Gypsum (calcium sulphate) binder.
2. **Why are plates activated?** Heating removes adsorbed water and makes the adsorbent active.
3. **Why do disaccharides have lower Rf?** They are more polar and larger, so they are held more strongly.
4. **How are sugars detected?** Spray reagents such as aniline–diphenylamine–phosphoric acid or anisaldehyde–sulphuric acid with heating.
5. **Advantages of TLC over paper chromatography?** Faster, sharper spots, more sensitive, corrosive reagents can be used.
6. **What is HPTLC?** High-performance TLC with finer particles, automatic application and densitometric scanning for quantitation.

# Separation of plant pigments by column chromatography

**Aim:** To separate the pigments of green leaves (carotenes, xanthophylls and chlorophylls) by adsorption column chromatography.

> Quantities and adsorbent are typical for a student batch; some laboratories use alumina or powdered sucrose instead of silica gel. Follow your lab manual and your teacher. Petroleum ether and acetone are highly flammable: no flames nearby.

## Principle

Leaf extract contains pigments of different polarity. When it is passed through a column of a polar adsorbent, the pigments are adsorbed to different extents and form separate coloured bands. They are eluted with solvents of increasing polarity. The **least polar** pigments (carotenes, hydrocarbons) are held weakly and come out first with petroleum ether; **xanthophylls** (oxygenated carotenoids) come next; **chlorophyll a** and the more polar **chlorophyll b** are held most and need more polar solvent. This is the type of experiment with which Tswett first described chromatography.

| Pigment | Colour | Polarity | Elution order |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| β-Carotene | Orange-yellow | Lowest | First |
| Xanthophylls (lutein) | Yellow | Higher | Second |
| Chlorophyll a | Blue-green | Higher | Third |
| Chlorophyll b | Yellow-green | Highest | Last |

## Requirements

Chromatography column (glass tube with stopcock, about 30 cm × 1.5 cm), glass wool, sand, mortar and pestle, separating funnel, beakers, test tubes; fresh green leaves (spinach), acetone, petroleum ether (60–80 °C), silica gel (column grade) or alumina, anhydrous sodium sulphate.

## Procedure

1. **Extract:** grind about 5 g of washed leaves with 20 ml acetone (a little sand helps). Filter. Shake the filtrate with 20 ml petroleum ether and water in a separating funnel; keep the upper petroleum ether layer (pigments), dry it over anhydrous sodium sulphate and concentrate to a few ml in a warm water bath (no flame).
2. **Column:** plug the bottom with glass wool and add a little sand. Make a slurry of adsorbent in petroleum ether and pour it in, tapping gently so that it settles evenly without air bubbles or cracks (wet packing). Add a thin layer of sand on top. Never let the column run dry.
3. **Loading:** drain the solvent to just above the sand; add the concentrated extract carefully as a narrow band.
4. **Elution:** elute with petroleum ether; collect the first orange-yellow band (carotenes).
5. Change to petroleum ether containing a small proportion of acetone (for example 9 : 1 then 7 : 3) to elute the yellow xanthophylls and then the green chlorophylls; collect each coloured band in a separate tube.
6. Note the colour, order of elution and approximate volume of each fraction.
7. Optionally check the purity of each fraction by TLC or record its visible spectrum.

## Observations

> Example observations, for practice only — record your own.

| Fraction | Eluting solvent | Colour of band | Pigment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Petroleum ether | Orange-yellow | Carotenes |
| 2 | Petroleum ether : acetone (9 : 1) | Yellow | Xanthophylls |
| 3 | Petroleum ether : acetone (7 : 3) | Blue-green | Chlorophyll a |
| 4 | More acetone (or acetone alone) | Yellow-green | Chlorophyll b |

## Result

The leaf pigments were separated into ___ bands, eluted in the order carotenes → xanthophylls → chlorophyll a → chlorophyll b.

## Precautions

1. Pack the column evenly with a slurry; air bubbles and cracks cause uneven bands.
2. Never allow the solvent level to fall below the top of the adsorbent.
3. Apply the sample as a thin, even band.
4. Increase solvent polarity gradually.
5. Work away from flames and in a ventilated area; pigments are light-sensitive, so work quickly.

## Viva questions

1. **Why does carotene elute first?** It is a non-polar hydrocarbon and is held least by the polar adsorbent.
2. **What is the principle of this separation?** Adsorption chromatography with stepwise (gradient) elution.
3. **What is the eluotropic series?** Order of solvents by increasing eluting power on a polar adsorbent.
4. **Why is wet packing preferred?** It gives an even bed without trapped air or cracks.
5. **Who first separated leaf pigments by chromatography?** Tswett (1906), on a calcium carbonate column.
6. **How can fraction purity be checked?** By TLC or by recording the visible absorption spectrum.

# Demonstration experiment on HPLC

**Aim:** To study the parts and operation of a high performance liquid chromatograph, record the chromatogram of a drug mixture (for example paracetamol and caffeine) by reversed-phase HPLC, and calculate system suitability parameters and the content of a sample.

> This is a demonstration; the conditions below are typical examples. Use the method your teacher sets up and the instrument instructions. Wear goggles and gloves; methanol and acetonitrile are toxic and flammable.

## Principle

In reversed-phase HPLC the stationary phase is non-polar (octadecylsilane, C18, bonded to silica) and the mobile phase is polar (water or buffer with methanol or acetonitrile), pumped at high pressure. Polar compounds spend less time in the stationary phase and elute first; less polar ones are retained longer. A UV detector records the eluate, giving peaks whose **retention time** identifies a compound and whose **area** is proportional to its amount.

```text
 [Mobile phase] -> [Degasser] -> [Pump] -> [Injector, 20 µl loop] -> [Guard + C18 column] -> [UV detector] -> [Data system]
```

## Requirements (typical)

HPLC system with pump, Rheodyne (or auto) injector with 20 µl loop, C18 column (250 × 4.6 mm, 5 µm), UV detector, data system; 0.45 µm membrane filters, syringe filters, sonicator, volumetric flasks; HPLC-grade methanol and water; paracetamol and caffeine reference standards, sample (tablet solution).

Example conditions: mobile phase methanol : water (about 25 : 75 v/v), flow 1.0 ml/min, detection at about 254 nm (or as set), column at room temperature or 30 °C, injection 20 µl.

## Procedure

1. **Mobile phase:** mix the solvents, filter through a 0.45 µm membrane and degas (sonication or helium sparging).
2. **System start-up:** prime the pump, start the flow at 1.0 ml/min and equilibrate the column until the pressure and baseline are steady (note the back-pressure).
3. **Standard solution:** prepare a mixed standard (for example 20 µg/ml of each drug) in mobile phase; filter through a 0.45 µm syringe filter.
4. **Sample solution:** prepare from tablet powder to the same nominal concentration; filter.
5. **System suitability:** inject the standard six times (load the loop in the "load" position, turn to "inject").
6. Inject the sample (in duplicate).
7. Note retention times, peak areas, peak widths and tailing from the data system.
8. Calculate k, α, N, Rs, tailing factor and %RSD; calculate the sample content by the external standard method.
9. **Shut-down:** wash the column with a higher proportion of organic solvent (for example methanol : water 80 : 20) if buffers were used, then stop the flow.

## Observations and calculations

> Example readings, for practice only — record your own.

Dead time t0 = 1.5 min (solvent front).

| Peak | tR (min) | Base width W (min) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paracetamol (A) | 4.2 | 0.30 |
| Caffeine (B) | 5.6 | 0.34 |

- Capacity factors: kA = (4.2 − 1.5)/1.5 = **1.80**; kB = (5.6 − 1.5)/1.5 = **2.73**.
- Selectivity: α = 2.73/1.80 = **1.52**.
- Resolution: Rs = 2(5.6 − 4.2)/(0.30 + 0.34) = 2.8/0.64 = **4.37** (baseline separation; must be at least 1.5, or as stated in the monograph).
- Theoretical plates (caffeine): N = 16(5.6/0.34)² = **4340**.
- Tailing factor (example: width at 5% height 0.14 min, front half-width 0.06 min): T = 0.14/(2 × 0.06) = **1.17** (limit usually not more than 2.0).

**Replicate standard injections (paracetamol peak areas):** 152340, 151890, 152760, 152110, 151950, 152480.
Mean = 152,255; SD = 335; **%RSD = 0.22%** (usual limit not more than 2.0%).

**Assay (external standard):** standard 20 µg/ml gives mean area 152,255; sample area 148,900.
c_sample = 20 × 148,900/152,255 = **19.56 µg/ml**, that is 19.56/20 × 100 = **97.8%** of the nominal concentration. Convert to mg per tablet using the dilution scheme.

## Result

1. Retention times: paracetamol ___ min, caffeine ___ min.
2. System suitability: N = ___, Rs = ___, T = ___, %RSD = ___ (within / outside limits).
3. The sample contains ___% of the labelled amount.

## Precautions

1. Use only HPLC-grade, filtered and degassed solvents.
2. Never let the pump run dry; prime it to remove air.
3. Filter all samples to protect the column; use a guard column.
4. Do not exceed the column's pressure and pH limits (silica C18 is usually used between pH 2 and 8).
5. Flush buffers out of the system after use.
6. Use the same injection volume and conditions for standards and samples.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is it called reversed phase?** The stationary phase is non-polar and the mobile phase polar, the reverse of classical normal-phase chromatography.
2. **Which drug elutes first and why?** The more polar one (paracetamol), because it is held less by C18.
3. **Why is the mobile phase degassed?** Bubbles cause pump and detector problems (pressure fluctuation, noisy baseline).
4. **What is system suitability?** Checks (RSD, plates, tailing, resolution) that show the system works properly before samples are analysed.
5. **What does the guard column do?** Protects the analytical column from particles and strongly retained material.
6. **Name HPLC detectors.** UV-visible, PDA, fluorescence, refractive index, electrochemical, mass spectrometer.

# Demonstration experiment on gas chromatography

**Aim:** To study the parts and working of a gas chromatograph, record the chromatogram of a mixture of volatile alcohols, and calculate column parameters, percentage composition by area normalisation and ethanol content by the internal standard method.

> This is a demonstration; the conditions below are typical examples. Use the method your teacher sets up and the instrument instructions. Carrier and fuel gas cylinders must be handled only by trained staff; hydrogen is flammable.

## Principle

In gas–liquid chromatography the sample is vaporised in a heated injection port and carried by an inert gas through a column containing a liquid stationary phase. Components separate according to their volatility and their interaction with the stationary phase; each leaves the column at its own **retention time**. A **flame ionisation detector (FID)** burns the eluate in a hydrogen–air flame; organic compounds produce ions and a current proportional to the amount of carbon reaching the flame. Peak area is used for quantitation.

```text
 [N2/He cylinder] -> [Regulator + flow control] -> [Heated injector] -> [Column in oven] -> [FID (H2 + air)] -> [Data system]
```

## Requirements (typical)

Gas chromatograph with FID, capillary column (for example polyethylene glycol type, 30 m × 0.32 mm) or packed column, carrier gas (nitrogen or helium), hydrogen and air for the FID, microsyringe (1–10 µl); methanol, ethanol, isopropanol, n-propanol (internal standard), water, sample (for example a hydroalcoholic preparation).

Example conditions: injector 200 °C, detector 250 °C, oven 60 °C isothermal (or programmed 40 → 150 °C at 10 °C/min), split ratio 1 : 50, injection 1 µl.

## Procedure

1. Check gas supplies; set carrier gas flow and the hydrogen and air flows for the FID; ignite the flame.
2. Set injector, oven and detector temperatures and wait for a steady baseline.
3. **Identification:** inject each alcohol separately (diluted in water) and note its retention time.
4. **Mixture:** inject the mixture and note the separated peaks.
5. **Internal standard method for ethanol:** prepare a standard containing 5% v/v ethanol and a fixed amount of n-propanol; prepare the sample with the same amount of n-propanol. Inject each and record the areas of ethanol and n-propanol.
6. Calculate resolution, plates, capacity factor, % composition and ethanol content.
7. After use, lower the oven temperature, switch off the flame gases and then the carrier gas as instructed.

## Observations and calculations

> Example readings, for practice only — record your own.

**Column parameters** (air peak t0 = 0.9 min):

| Peak | tR (min) | W (min) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ethanol | 2.8 | 0.12 |
| Isopropanol | 3.4 | 0.14 |

- k (ethanol) = (2.8 − 0.9)/0.9 = **2.11**
- Rs = 2(3.4 − 2.8)/(0.12 + 0.14) = 1.2/0.26 = **4.6**
- N (isopropanol) = 16(3.4/0.14)² = **9440 plates**

**Area normalisation** (peaks of similar response):

| Component | Area | % = area/total × 100 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Methanol | 2150 | 4.3 |
| Ethanol | 46,800 | 93.6 |
| Isopropanol | 1050 | 2.1 |
| Total | 50,000 | 100 |

**Internal standard method:**

- Standard (5.0% v/v ethanol): ethanol area 38,000, n-propanol area 40,000; ratio = 0.950.
- Sample: ethanol area 36,100, n-propanol area 40,500; ratio = 0.891.
- Ethanol in sample = 5.0 × 0.891/0.950 = **4.69% v/v**.

## Result

1. Retention times: methanol ___, ethanol ___, isopropanol ___ min.
2. Rs = ___, N = ___.
3. The sample contains ___% v/v ethanol.

## Precautions

1. Never heat the column or detector without carrier gas flowing.
2. Rinse the syringe with the next sample; inject quickly and smoothly to the same depth.
3. Replace the septum regularly to avoid leaks.
4. Keep the injector hotter than the boiling point of the least volatile component.
5. Check that the FID flame is lit before injecting.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the mobile phase in GC?** An inert carrier gas such as nitrogen, helium or hydrogen.
2. **Why is FID widely used?** It is sensitive to almost all organic compounds and has a wide linear range; it does not respond to water.
3. **Why use an internal standard?** It corrects for small differences in injected volume.
4. **What is temperature programming?** Raising the oven temperature during the run to elute wide-boiling mixtures as sharp peaks.
5. **Which compounds cannot be analysed directly by GC?** Non-volatile or heat-unstable ones; they may need derivatization.
6. **Give a pharmacopoeial use of GC.** Residual solvents (headspace GC), ethanol content in tinctures.
practicals.title: Demonstration experiment on gas chromatography

1. Statement: when monochromatic light passes through a solution, absorbance is proportional to path length (Lambert) and concentration (Beer): A = log(I0/I) = εbc.
2. Terms: I0 incident, I transmitted intensity; T = I/I0; A = −log T = 2 − log %T; ε molar absorptivity (L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹); b path length (cm); c concentration; A(1%, 1 cm) for c in g/100 ml; ε = A(1%, 1 cm) × M/10.
3. Derivation: for a thin layer db, −dI/I = k c db; integrate from I0 to I and 0 to b: ln(I0/I) = kcb; convert to log: log(I0/I) = (k/2.303)cb = εbc.
4. Real deviations: concentration above about 0.01 M, interactions between molecules, change of refractive index.
5. Chemical deviations: association, dissociation, complexation or reaction with solvent; dichromate–chromate equilibrium with pH; benzoic acid dimers; remedy by buffering or measuring at the isosbestic point.
6. Instrumental deviations: polychromatic radiation, stray light, wide slits, mismatched or dirty cells, detector non-linearity, fluorescence of sample.
7. Positive vs negative deviation sketch (curve bending up or toward the concentration axis).
8. Example: ε = 15,000, A = 0.45, b = 1 cm → c = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ M. Keep A within 0.2–0.8.
